info.bio:
Admirador confeso de Bob Dylan, Van Morrison y los Rolling Stones, Graham Parker es uno de los grandes nombres aparecidos en el denominado circuito pub-rock británico de los años 70, bandas y solistas que intentaban recupera la esencia básica del rock’n’roll y los sonidos tradicionales del blues, R&B, soul o country.

Graham Parker (nacido el 18 de noviembre de 1950 en Londres), un antiguo gasolinero y criador de cobayas, principió en esto de la música interpretando soul y R&B en bandas como The Black Rockers y Deep Cut Three.

scenes.name: British Graffiti: pub-rock y mods
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Gran Bretaña tenía los pubs: el renacimiento nace de los músicos que tocaban rhythm'n'blues y rockabilly en ellos, y el punk les saca de allí. Surge un nuevo cantautor, anclado en las raíces y consciente de lo social: Dave Edmunds, Nick Lowe, Graham Parker, Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello (el «joven airado» de la new wave, quizá sobrevalorado), Tom Robinson, Ian Dury, Wreckless Eric. Dire Straits; el revival mod de los Jam y los Television Personalities; los Soft Boys de Robyn Hitchcock, cimiento del revival psicodélico; Boomtown Rats, Undertones, Bananarama.

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …there emerged a new kind of singer-songwriter, solidly anchored to the roots of rock'n'roll and aware of social issues. Dave Edmunds, Nick Lowe, Graham Parker, Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello, and Tom Robinson, not to mention the demented Ian Dury and the even more demented Wreckless Eric, were the bards who…

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …frequency, though. Nick Lowe (1) was the theoretician of power-pop and American roots-rock, as evidenced already on Jesus Of Cool (1978), while Graham Parker (1) was fundamentally a disciple of Bruce Springsteen, Van Morrison and Neil Young, as revealed by Squeezing Out 130

podcast.title: "Alternative Godfather" Status
podcast.body: For a brief period, Graham Parker was welcomed at Modern Rock Radio as a kind of "alternative Godfather." This recognition came with the launch of Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart in 1988, on which his song "Don't Let Them Break You Down" appeared, and was further solidified by subsequent chart success. "For a brief time, Parker was welcomed at Modern Rock Radio as a kind of alternative Godfather."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Angry Young Men" Figure
podcast.body: Parker gained acclaim from critics and tastemakers, becoming known as one of the "Angry Young Men." This was an ironic title, considering he was often as "tender and soulful as much as they were angry," but the name nonetheless stuck. He became a central figure, or "locus," of what New Wave evolved into, emerging from England's pub rock and punk rock scenes and the transatlantic sound of Power Pop. "Graham Parker."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: "Angry Young Men" Moniker
podcast.body: Along with Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson, Graham Parker was among a group of British singer-songwriters who emerged from Pub Rock and Powerpop, adopted a punk attitude, helped shape new wave, and were collectively tagged with the moniker "Angry Young Men." This label characterized their early careers but became less fitting as they evolved their sound in the early 1980s. "and were tagged with the moniker, Angry Young Men."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Angry Young Man
podcast.body: Graham Parker was known as an "Angry Young Man" within the New Wave rock scene. "New Wave Rocker and so-called Angry Young Man Graham Parker, dist his record label Mercury on the Asurbic Butt Catchy Mercury Poisoning."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Aspirations as "Next Bruce Springsteen"
podcast.body: Arista Records, eager to replicate the success of Bruce Springsteen, connected Graham Parker and The Rumour with producer Jimmy Iovine, known for his work with Springsteen. This move aimed to position Parker as a major mainstream rock artist, although critics later noted Iovine's production "neutered The Rumour's raucous sound." "Arresta Records, eager to make him the next Bruce Springsteen, connected Parker and the rumor with producer Jimmy Iaveen."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Disputes with Mercury Records
podcast.body: Parker grew convinced that his US label, Mercury Records, was "botching his career" due to their struggles to promote him effectively, resulting in singles failing to reach the Hot 100 and albums languishing at the bottom of the charts. This frustration led him to fulfill his contract with the contemptuous live album *The Parkerilla* and record the outspoken diss track "Mercury Poisoning." "Parker came to believe Mercury was botching his career."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Early Life and Work Experience
podcast.body: Born in Hackney, East London in 1950, Parker spent the early 1970s working various jobs such as factory worker, dock worker, and gas station attendant, while simultaneously performing in obscure pub rock bands around London. "Graham Thomas Parker, born in Hackney, East London in 1950, spent the early 70s working on jobs, factory worker, dock worker, gas station attendant, and gigging around London in obscure pub rock bands."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Musical Evolution in the 80s
podcast.body: In the 1980s, Parker would evolve to become "wistful," reinventing the New Wave template and achieving new pop heights. His music would no longer be confined to punk, post punk, or power pop. "Graham turns wistful."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Musical Influences
podcast.body: His distinctive sound drew inspiration from artists like Van Morrison and 1960s R&B, leading it to be characterized as "white soul crossed with pub rock." "Parker's sound drew inspiration from the likes of Van Morrison and 60s R&B."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Playing Himself in "This Is 40"
podcast.body: Graham Parker, with his sense of humor about his career, played himself in the 2012 Judd Apatow comedy "This Is 40." In the film, Paul Rudd's character, an indie record label owner, signs Parker and reunites The Rumour in an attempt to finally get them the hit they deserved. "He had enough of a sense of humor about this to play himself in the 2012 Judd Appetal comedy This Is 40."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Switching Record Labels and Artistic Integrity
podcast.body: Graham Parker exhibited strong will and artistic integrity, switching record companies multiple times over just one album ("The Mona Lisa's Sister") because he refused to compromise on his vision. He left Atlantic Records after they insisted on outside producers and studio sheen, then signed with RCA to produce the album himself with The Rumour for under $60,000. "Graham Parker was perhaps the most willful of all, switching record companies two more times over just one album that he refused to compromise on."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Touring with Sola
podcast.body: At some point, when The Rumour could not be afforded to fly in, Graham Parker toured with a different backing act called Sola, indicating pragmatic adaptations for live performances. "And tonight we have Sola because we couldn't afford to fly in the rumor."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Uphill Commercial Battle
podcast.body: Throughout his career, Graham Parker consistently faced an uphill battle for commercial success, with chart victories often being small and hard-won. This struggle persisted despite critical acclaim and efforts by his labels to push him into the mainstream. "Commerciale, Graham Parker was always facing an uphill battle. Chart victories were small and hard one."
